summary: The Hoop stress calculator turns the length of the shell, the thickness to diameter ratio, the poisson's ratio and the efficiency of the circumferential joint into shell diameter (d). That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Hoop stress calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hoop stress calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports shell diameter (d) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the shape); then you type in the length of the shell (l), the thickness to diameter ratio (t/d), the poisson's ratio (μ) and the efficiency of the circumferential joint (ηc).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hoop stress calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Shell diameter (d)=2 × shell radius (r)
Thickness of the shell (t)=shell diameter (d) × thickness to diameter ratio (t ÷ d)
Hoop stress (σₕ)=internal pressure (P) × shell radius (r) ÷ (efficiency of the longitudinal riveted joint (ηₜ) × thickness of the shell (t))
Internal pressure (P)=2 × efficiency of the circumferential joint (ηc) × longitudinal stress (σₕ) × thickness of the shell (t) ÷ shell radius (r)
Efficiency of the circumferential joint (η)=(1 ÷ 2) × internal pressure (P) × shell radius (r) ÷ (hoop stress (σₕ) × thickness of the shell (t))
Internal pressure (P)=-2 × radial stress (σr)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Shape set to Sphere, Shell radius (r) = 30 mm, Efficiency of the circumferential joint (ηc) = 1 and Efficiency of the longitudinal riveted joint (ηₜ) = 1. Working through the relationship above gives Shell diameter (d) = 60 mm.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Shell diameter (d) = 60 mm should be roughly the size you expected from Shape set to Sphere and Shell radius (r) = 30 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hoop stress calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length of the shell, the thickness to diameter ratio and the poisson's ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hoop stress calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns shell diameter (d), derived from the length of the shell, the thickness to diameter ratio and the poisson's ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hoop stress calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length of the shell, the thickness to diameter ratio, the poisson's ratio and the efficiency of the circumferential joint, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter shell radius (r) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Shell radius (r) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Shell diameter (d) = 60 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hoop stress calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
